pests.name: Spittlebug
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Frothy white spit-like foam on stems in late spring, with the small nymph hidden inside. It looks alarming but rarely harms an established lavender plant.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Blobs of white froth that look like spit on the stems in late spring, with a tiny bug hidden inside. It looks worse than it is.
pests.cause_seasoned: Spittlebug nymphs, which shelter inside their own foam while feeding on plant sap. Numbers are usually low and the damage is mostly cosmetic.
pests.cause_beginner: Young spittlebugs hiding in the foam while they feed. There are usually only a few, and they do little real harm.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock them off with a strong spray of water if you find them unsightly. No treatment is needed for plant health in most cases.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: If the froth bothers you, spray it off with a hose. You usually do not need to do anything else.
pests.prevention_seasoned: No specific prevention is warranted. Keeping plants spaced for airflow and not overwatering keeps lavender vigorous enough to shrug off minor pests.
pests.prevention_beginner: Nothing special is needed. Giving plants room and not overwatering keeps lavender healthy enough to handle small pests.

pests.name: Whiteflies and aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Occasional clusters of tiny white flies or soft aphids on new growth, most likely on stressed or overcrowded plants in poor conditions rather than on healthy lavender.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Now and then, tiny white flies or small soft bugs on new growth, usually only on plants that are stressed or too crowded.
pests.cause_seasoned: Sap-feeding insects that occasionally find lavender. Lavender has few pests overall and is typically grown with little or no pesticide.
pests.cause_beginner: Small sap-sucking insects that sometimes show up. Lavender has very few pest problems and rarely needs spraying.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rinse them off with water or use insecticidal soap if numbers climb. Removing nearby stressors and improving airflow usually resolves it.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray them off with water, or use insecticidal soap if there are a lot. Giving the plant more air and removing stress usually fixes it.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Give plants full sun, lean soil, and good spacing, and avoid overwatering. Vigorous, unstressed lavender rarely attracts these pests.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep lavender in full sun with room around it, dry lean soil, and not too much water. Healthy plants rarely get these bugs.

diseases.name: Phytophthora root and crown rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellowing, wilting, and dieback that does not recover with watering, often with a darkened, decayed crown at the soil line. It is the disease of concern for lavender and is tied to wet conditions and poor drainage.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Leaves yellow and the plant wilts and dies back even though the soil is wet, often with a dark, rotted spot where the stems meet the ground. This is the main disease that kills lavender, and it comes from staying too wet.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Water mold pathogens that thrive in saturated, poorly drained soil and attack the roots and crown. Wet feet, not cold, is the underlying cause.
diseases.cause_beginner: A rot that takes hold when soil stays soggy and drains badly, attacking the roots and base. The real cause is wet soil, not cold weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once the crown is rotting; remove and discard affected plants. Focus everything on prevention through drainage rather than rescue.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Once the base is rotting there is no fix, so pull out and throw away affected plants. The answer is preventing it with good drainage, not curing it.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant in sharply drained soil in full sun, water deeply but infrequently, and never let lavender sit in wet ground. On clay, use a mound or raised bed, and space plants for airflow.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant in well-draining soil in full sun, water deeply but rarely, and never let lavender sit in soggy ground. On heavy clay, plant on a mound or raised bed and give plants room.

diseases.name: Leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small spots or blotches on the foliage, more likely in humid weather or on crowded, poorly ventilated plants. It is a minor issue compared with root and crown rot.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small spots on the leaves, more likely in damp weather or on crowded plants. It is a minor problem next to root rot.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Foliar fungi favored by damp, still air around the plant. Crowding and overhead watering raise the risk.
diseases.cause_beginner: Leaf fungi that like damp, still air around the plant. Crowding and watering from above make it worse.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected foliage, improve airflow, and water at the base rather than overhead. The annual cut-back also helps clear and renew the canopy.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick off the spotted leaves, give the plant more air, and water at the soil instead of over the top. The yearly trim helps too.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants at least 2 to 3 feet apart for air circulation, site in full sun, and avoid overhead watering. Good airflow is the main defense.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Leave 2 to 3 feet between plants for airflow, plant in full sun, and avoid watering over the leaves. Good air movement is the main thing.

pests.name: Generally pest-resistant (aromatic-oil deterrence)
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Healthy in-ground lemongrass rarely shows insect damage. Extension guides describe it as essentially free of pest problems when grown well, an effect attributed to the citral-rich essential oils in its foliage that repel many insects. Scattered chewing or a few sap-feeders may appear on stressed or crowded plants but seldom rise to a real infestation outdoors.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Lemongrass is one of the least pest-troubled herbs you can grow. Its own lemony oils keep most bugs away, so outdoor plants usually look clean.
pests.cause_seasoned: The plant's aromatic oils (notably citral) are used in insect-repellent products. Robust, well-watered clumps in full sun are the least attractive to pests; stress and crowding are what invite occasional trouble.
pests.cause_beginner: Lemongrass makes lemony oils that many insects dislike, so it is naturally left alone. Keeping it healthy and unstressed keeps it that way.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rarely needed outdoors. For the occasional sap-feeder, a strong jet of water or an insecticidal soap spray is sufficient. Remove and destroy badly damaged outer leaves. Improving airflow and vigor usually resolves minor issues without any product.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: You will seldom need to treat lemongrass. If you do see a few bugs, blast them off with water or use an insecticidal soap. Trim off any damaged leaves.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Grow in full sun with rich soil and steady water to keep clumps vigorous, and divide crowded clumps so air moves through them. Vigorous plants are the best defense.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep lemongrass healthy with sun, rich soil, and plenty of water, and divide it when it gets crowded. A strong plant rarely has pest trouble.

pests.name: Spider mites (indoor and hot, dry conditions)
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine stippling or a dusty, faded look on the leaf blades, sometimes with delicate webbing where the leaf meets the stem, most often on plants overwintered indoors or grown in hot, dry, stagnant air. Heavy feeding bronzes and dries the foliage.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny specks and a faded, dusty look on the leaves, sometimes with fine webbing. This shows up mostly on plants kept indoors over winter.
pests.cause_seasoned: Spider mites (Tetranychidae) thrive in the warm, dry, low-airflow conditions of a heated indoor room, which is exactly where potted lemongrass spends the winter. They are far less of a problem on well-watered outdoor clumps.
pests.cause_beginner: Spider mites are tiny pests that love warm, dry indoor air. They tend to appear on lemongrass that is overwintering inside.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rinse the foliage with a strong spray of water, raise humidity around indoor plants, and treat persistent infestations with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil, covering the leaf undersides. Cutting the plant back hard before bringing it indoors reduces the mite population it carries in.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray the leaves with water to knock mites off and raise the humidity around indoor plants. For stubborn cases, use insecticidal soap. Cutting the plant back before bringing it inside helps a lot.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Before overwintering, cut the plant back and inspect it, and keep indoor humidity up with misting or a nearby water tray. Avoid hot, dry, stagnant spots for indoor pots.
pests.prevention_beginner: Before bringing lemongrass indoors, trim it back and check it over. Keep the indoor air from getting too hot and dry by misting now and then.

diseases.name: Lemongrass rust
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small chlorotic (yellow) flecks appear on both leaf surfaces and enlarge into reddish to crimson streaks; on the leaf underside these rupture into powdery orange-brown pustules. Severe infection produces large patches of tan to purplish dead tissue and dries the leaves, cutting yield and quality. It is favored by warm, humid weather and crowded, poorly ventilated plantings.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Yellow flecks that turn into reddish streaks, plus orange-brown powdery spots on the undersides of the leaves. Bad cases dry the leaves out. It shows up most in warm, humid, crowded conditions.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Rust caused by the fungus Puccinia nakanishikii, the most notable disease of lemongrass in humid tropical and subtropical areas; the University of Hawaii CTAHR documents it, and it has been reported on Florida lemongrass. Spores spread on wind and splashing water, and dense, wet, still canopies favor infection.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus called rust, spread by wind and splashing water. It is most common where it is warm, humid, and the plants are packed close together.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy heavily infected leaves to reduce spore load, and open the clump up by dividing and thinning to improve airflow. Water at the base rather than overhead so leaves dry quickly. Copper-based fungicides can be used preventively where rust pressure is high; culture is the primary control.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Cut off and throw away badly spotted leaves, and thin or divide crowded clumps so air moves through. Water at the base, not over the leaves. A copper fungicide can help if rust is a recurring problem.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space and divide clumps for good air movement, water at the soil line to keep foliage dry, and avoid overhead irrigation in humid weather. Vigorous, uncrowded plants in full sun resist rust best.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Give plants room, divide crowded clumps, and water at the base so the leaves stay dry. Good airflow and full sun are the best prevention.

diseases.name: Leaf blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Brown, elongated lesions develop along the leaf blades in warm, wet weather and can spread quickly through dense plantings, browning and drying the foliage from the tips and margins inward.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Brown streaks and dead patches on the leaves during warm, wet spells. In crowded plants it can spread fast.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A foliar leaf-blight fungus that is favored by prolonged leaf wetness, high humidity, and crowding. As with rust, still, wet canopies drive it, and it is the second disease of note for lemongrass grown in humid regions.
diseases.cause_beginner: A leaf fungus that thrives when leaves stay wet and plants are packed together in warm, humid weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves, thin or divide crowded clumps, and switch to base watering to shorten leaf-wetness periods. Copper-based products can be used preventively under heavy pressure.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Trim off the blighted leaves, thin crowded clumps, and water at the base instead of over the top. A copper spray can help in bad cases.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Prioritize airflow (wide spacing, regular division) and dry foliage (base watering, morning irrigation). Avoid working in or harvesting from wet plants, which spreads spores.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Keep plants spaced and divided so air moves through, and water at the base so leaves dry fast. Try not to handle the plants while they are wet.

diseases.name: Root rot (overwatering in poor drainage)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellowing, wilting, and collapse of stalks despite wet soil, with soft, dark, decayed roots and stalk bases. It appears when a thirsty plant is grown in soil that stays waterlogged, especially in containers with poor drainage.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The plant yellows, wilts, and rots at the base even though the soil is wet. The roots turn soft and dark. This comes from soil that stays soggy.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Although lemongrass demands abundant water, its roots rot in soil that is chronically waterlogged. Soil-borne rot organisms take hold when drainage is poor or a pot sits in standing water, so drainage is as important as watering volume.
diseases.cause_beginner: Lemongrass loves water but hates sitting in it. If the soil or pot does not drain, the roots rot.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once roots are extensively rotted; remove affected plants. Improve drainage, repot into a free-draining mix, empty saucers after watering, and water generously but allow excess to drain freely.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot save a badly rotted plant, so remove it. Fix the drainage, repot into fresh mix if it is in a container, and never let the pot sit in standing water.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant in well-drained, organically rich soil; in containers use a free-draining mix and pots with ample holes, and empty the saucer after each watering. Water deeply and often, but let the excess escape.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Grow lemongrass in soil or a pot that drains well. Water it a lot, but make sure the extra water can run out and the pot never sits in a full saucer.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_beginner: Clusters of tiny soft green or gray insects on the growing tips and undersides of leaves, sometimes with curled, sticky foliage.
pests.cause_beginner: Aphids are small sap-sucking insects that breed fast, especially on soft growth from too much fertilizer, and they can spread plant viruses.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap or neem oil on the leaf undersides, repeating every few days. Rinse cut sprigs well before use.
pests.prevention_beginner: Welcome ladybugs and lacewings, go easy on nitrogen, and check new growth often.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Colonies on growing tips and leaf undersides, one of the pests UC IPM lists for mint; honeydew and the insects themselves contaminate a crop eaten fresh, and soft, overfed growth is the most susceptible.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several aphid species feed on mint; they reproduce rapidly and favor the lush growth that excess nitrogen and rich soil produce.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Dislodge colonies with a water jet or spray insecticidal soap or neem, covering leaf undersides, and repeat every few days; conserve ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitoid wasps.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Scout the tips early, avoid overfeeding, and conserve natural enemies; because you eat the leaves, lean toward a strong water spray before anything else.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms_beginner: A fine stippling or speckling on the leaves, sometimes with faint webbing on the undersides, worst in hot, dry weather. Leaves look dull, sandy, or bronzed.
pests.cause_beginner: Tiny sap-sucking mites, not true insects, that explode in hot, dry, dusty conditions and are easy to miss until the leaves are speckled.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray the undersides of the leaves with a strong jet of water to knock them off, keep the plant well watered, and use insecticidal soap or neem if they persist.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep mint evenly moist and mulched, since drought stress invites mites, and rinse dusty foliage in hot spells.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Twospotted and related spider mites, which UC IPM lists for mint, stipple the foliage with pale flecks and spin fine webbing on the undersides; they flare in hot, dry, dusty conditions and on drought-stressed plants, which is why mint's moisture love is also its best mite defense.
pests.cause_seasoned: Spider mites feeding with piercing mouthparts; populations build fastest in heat and drought and on dusty, water-stressed plants.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hose the undersides forcefully and repeat, maintain steady soil moisture, and apply insecticidal soap or a miticidal oil to the leaf undersides; conserve predatory mites and minute pirate bugs.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Do not let mint dry out or get dusty, mulch to hold moisture, and scout the undersides in hot weather when mites move fastest.

pests.name: Cutworms, mint flea beetles, and root-feeding pests
pests.symptoms_beginner: Young shoots cut off at the soil line, notched or shot-holed leaves, or plants that weaken and thin out from grubs feeding on the roots and rhizomes.
pests.cause_beginner: A mix of chewing pests, cutworms and mint flea beetles above ground and root-feeding larvae below, that damage leaves, stems, and the underground runners.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Handpick cutworms at dusk and use cardboard collars on new transplants, hose or handpick flea beetles, and keep the bed clean; dividing and resetting a tired patch in fresh ground breaks root-pest cycles.
pests.prevention_beginner: Clear plant debris where cutworms shelter, rotate a heavily infested patch to fresh ground, and keep plants vigorous so they outgrow light feeding.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Utah State lists flea beetles and cutworms among mint's insect pests; cutworms sever young shoots at the soil line and mint flea beetles chew small holes, while soil and rhizome feeders thin an established patch from below. On a home planting numbers are usually modest.
pests.cause_seasoned: A complex of foliage feeders (cutworms, mint flea beetle) and root/rhizome feeders (root and rhizome larvae); the perennial, spreading root mass is what harbors the below-ground stages.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Handpick and use collars against cutworms, dislodge flea beetles with water or row cover on new plantings, and manage root pests culturally by dividing and resetting the patch in clean soil; reserve any spray for the labeled edible-herb products.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Sanitize debris, keep plants vigorous, and reset an infested patch into fresh ground on a multi-year cycle, the same renewal that keeps mint from getting woody.

diseases.name: Mint rust
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small orange, yellow, or rust-brown powdery pustules on the undersides of the leaves and on the stems, with pale spots on the upper surface. Badly affected leaves curl, brown, and drop, and rusty leaves are not good to eat.
diseases.cause_beginner: A rust fungus, the signature mint disease, that thrives in warm, humid, crowded conditions and lives over on the roots and rhizomes from year to year.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick off and destroy rusted leaves as soon as you see them, thin and space plants for airflow, water at the soil line, and cut a badly infected patch to the ground; in a severe case, start a fresh planting from clean, rust-free cuttings in a new spot.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Space plants for good airflow, avoid wetting the foliage, keep the patch from getting congested, and start new plantings from clean stock.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Puccinia menthae, the classic mint rust: orange to brown powdery pustules on leaf undersides, stems, and petioles, with defoliation in a bad year (NC State lists rust among the main mint diseases). It overwinters in the rhizomes, so an infected patch reinfects itself, and warm humid crowding drives it.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The rust fungus Puccinia menthae, favored by warm, humid, crowded conditions and carried over in the root and rhizome mass.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy infected leaves, open up the planting for airflow, switch to soil-line watering, and mow or cut a heavily infected patch to the ground and clear the debris; renew from clean cuttings in fresh ground where it recurs. There is no reliable home cure once it is established.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Airflow, dry foliage, and uncongested spacing are the defenses; propagate only from rust-free plants and reset a chronically infected patch elsewhere.

diseases.name: Verticillium wilt
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Stunted, off-color plants whose lower leaves yellow and wilt, often on just one side of a stem, with whole shoots or plants dying back in warm weather. It does not wash off and there is no spray cure.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil-borne fungus that clogs the plant's water-conducting tissue; it builds up in the ground and is the disease that shortens the life of a mint patch.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure for an infected plant, so remove it. Start fresh plantings from clean cuttings in a new bed, and do not follow tomatoes, potatoes, or strawberries, which host the same fungus.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant clean stock in ground with no recent history of the disease, avoid siting mint after verticillium-susceptible crops, and move the patch to fresh ground every few years.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Verticillium wilt (a soilborne Verticillium), the disease that most limits mint's longevity: slow, bronze-cast spring growth, one-sided branch development, lower-leaf yellowing and wilt in warm or dry weather, and dieback. The Connecticut Experiment Station and Utah State both flag it for mint. The fungus persists in soil for years and has a wide host range, so it is managed by site selection and renewal, not treatment.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A soilborne Verticillium fungus that invades the vascular system; it survives for years in soil and infects many crops (tomato, potato, strawberry, other mints).
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rogue out affected plants and manage by prevention: propagate disease-free cuttings, establish new patches in clean ground away from prior verticillium hosts, and rotate the mint bed on a multi-year cycle where the disease appears.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Use clean stock, avoid ground that grew tomatoes, potatoes, eggplant, or strawberries, and reset the patch in fresh soil periodically, since there is no rescue for an infected plant.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew and anthracnose (leaf spot)
diseases.symptoms_beginner: A white, powdery dust on the leaves and stems (powdery mildew), or dark sunken spots and blotches on leaves and stems (anthracnose leaf spot). Heavily spotted or coated leaves are not good to eat.
diseases.cause_beginner: Fungal leaf diseases that spread in crowded, humid plantings and on wet foliage, worse where air does not move.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove affected leaves, thin the planting and water at the soil line to keep the leaves dry, and cut a badly hit patch back to encourage clean new growth.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Space for airflow, water at the base rather than overhead, and avoid crowding.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Powdery mildew (white powdery patches that brown and shrivel heavy foliage, listed for mint by UC IPM) and anthracnose or leaf spot (Utah State and NC State list leaf-spotting fungi for mint), both favored by crowded, humid conditions and wet leaves.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Foliar fungi (powdery mildew; anthracnose and other leaf-spot fungi) driven by high humidity, crowding, and prolonged leaf wetness.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Improve airflow by thinning and dividing, water at the soil line, remove infected foliage, and shear a badly affected patch to force clean regrowth; drip irrigation and avoiding overnight leaf wetness are the practical controls Utah State recommends.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Open the canopy, keep the foliage dry, and do not let the patch get congested; renew a chronically diseased stand from clean cuttings.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of small soft-bodied insects on tender new growth, most likely on young seedlings or stressed, crowded plants. Mature oregano's aroma tends to repel them, so this is usually a minor, early-season problem.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Small soft bugs grouped on new growth, usually on young seedlings or stressed plants. Grown oregano's scent tends to keep them away, so this is normally minor.
pests.cause_seasoned: Sap-feeding insects that occasionally find oregano, mainly at the seedling stage. Oregano has few pests overall and is typically grown with little or no pesticide.
pests.cause_beginner: Small sap-sucking insects that sometimes appear, mostly on young plants. Oregano has very few pest problems and rarely needs spraying.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock them off with a strong spray of water, and use insecticidal soap or neem if numbers climb. A hard harvest removes much of the infested growth at once.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray them off with water, and use insecticidal soap or neem if there are a lot. Cutting the plant back also removes most of them.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Give plants full sun, lean soil, and good spacing for airflow, and avoid overwatering. Vigorous, unstressed oregano rarely attracts aphids, and mature plants largely deter them.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep oregano in full sun with room around it, dry lean soil, and not too much water. Healthy, mature plants rarely get aphids.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine stippling or yellowing on the leaves with faint webbing on the stems, most likely in hot, dry weather or on stressed or indoor plants. Oregano is generally pest-resistant, so this is usually minor and weather-driven.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny yellow speckles on the leaves and faint webbing on the stems, usually in hot, dry weather or on indoor plants. Oregano rarely has pest trouble, so this is normally minor.
pests.cause_seasoned: Tiny sap-feeding mites that flare in hot, dry conditions and on plants grown indoors. Oregano has few pests overall and seldom needs treatment.
pests.cause_beginner: Very small sap-sucking mites that show up in hot, dry spells or indoors. Oregano has very few pest problems and rarely needs spraying.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rinse plants with a strong spray of water, and use insecticidal soap if numbers build. A hard harvest or shear removes much of the infested growth.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray them off with water, and use insecticidal soap if there are a lot. Cutting the plant back also removes most of them.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Give plants full sun and good airflow, and do not let container plants bake bone-dry in a heat wave. Vigorous, unstressed oregano rarely attracts mites.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep oregano in full sun with room around it, and do not let potted plants dry out completely in a heat wave. Healthy plants rarely get mites.

diseases.name: Root and stem rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Gradual wilting, yellowing, and dieback that does not recover with watering, often with brown or black decay at the base of the stems and roots. It is the main way oregano is lost and is tied to wet, poorly drained soil and excess winter moisture rather than to cold.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The plant slowly wilts, yellows, and dies back even though the soil is wet, often with dark, rotted stems and roots at the base. This is the main thing that kills oregano, and it comes from soggy soil, not cold weather.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soilborne root and stem rots that thrive in saturated, poorly drained soil and attack the roots and stem base. Waterlogged ground and wet winters, not cold, are the underlying cause; oregano is intolerant of wet feet.
diseases.cause_beginner: Rots that take hold when soil stays soggy and drains badly, attacking the roots and base of the stems. The real cause is wet soil, not cold, and it is worst over a wet winter.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once the crown and roots are rotting; remove and discard affected plants. Focus everything on prevention through drainage rather than rescue.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Once the base is rotting there is no fix, so pull out and throw away affected plants. The answer is preventing it with good drainage, not curing it.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, keep plants on the dry side, and never let oregano sit in wet ground or excess winter moisture. On clay or in humid regions, use a mound or raised bed and space plants for airflow.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant in fast-draining soil in full sun, keep it on the dry side, and never let oregano sit in soggy ground, especially over winter. On heavy clay or in humid areas, plant on a mound or raised bed and give plants room.

diseases.name: Rust
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small circular spots and orange or brown powdery pustules on the leaves and stems, a rust fungus that can spread through a planting if left unchecked. Caught early, pruning off affected parts can save the plant.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small round spots and rusty orange or brown powder on the leaves and stems. This is a rust disease, and if you catch it early, cutting off the affected parts can save the plant.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A rust fungus favored by damp, crowded, poorly ventilated conditions and overhead watering. Oregano can be affected when the foliage stays wet.
diseases.cause_beginner: A rust fungus that likes damp, crowded plants and wet leaves. Oregano can catch it when the foliage stays wet.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune out and destroy affected growth promptly, improve airflow, and water at the base rather than overhead. Severely infected plants are best removed to protect the rest.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Cut off and throw away the affected parts, give the plant more air, and water at the soil instead of over the top. Badly infected plants are best pulled out.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants for good air circulation, site in full sun, avoid overhead watering, and remove plant debris. Good airflow and dry foliage are the main defenses.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Give plants room for airflow, plant in full sun, and avoid watering over the leaves. Keeping the foliage dry and the area tidy is the main thing.

diseases.name: Botrytis and humid-weather foliar disease
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Grayish moldy patches, spotting, or a powdery-white coating on the foliage, favored by warm, humid, still air and on crowded or overhead-watered plants. A minor issue next to root and stem rot.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Grayish mold, spots, or a powdery white film on the leaves in warm, humid weather, more likely on crowded plants. A minor problem next to root rot.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Foliar fungi such as Botrytis (gray mold) and powdery mildew that are favored by humidity, crowding, and poor air movement. Oregano is fairly disease-resistant, so these are mainly a humid-climate and overcrowding issue.
diseases.cause_beginner: Leaf fungi like gray mold and powdery mildew that like damp, still, humid air and crowded plants. Oregano is fairly disease-resistant, so this is mostly a humid-weather problem.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected foliage, open up airflow, and water at the base rather than overhead. A hard harvest or shear clears and renews the canopy.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick off affected leaves, give the plant more air, and water at the soil instead of over the top. Cutting it back also helps.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants for air circulation, site in full sun, avoid overhead watering, and favor upright culinary types over dense low ones where humidity is high. Good airflow is the main defense.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Give plants room for airflow, plant in full sun, and avoid watering over the leaves. In humid areas, more open upright plants handle it better than dense low mats.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine stippling, dull or bronzed needles, and faint webbing, most common in hot, dry weather and especially on plants overwintered indoors in dry heat.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Leaves look dusty, dull, or speckled, sometimes with fine webbing, usually in hot dry spells or on a plant kept indoors over winter.
pests.cause_seasoned: Tiny sap-feeding mites that thrive in dry conditions. Dry indoor air over winter is a classic trigger, and drought-stressed outdoor plants are also vulnerable.
pests.cause_beginner: Very small mites that love dry air and dry, stressed plants. They flare up most on rosemary brought indoors for winter.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rinse plants with a strong stream of water regularly, raise humidity around indoor plants, and use insecticidal soap or horticultural oil if numbers climb. Keeping the plant unstressed is the main defense.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray the plant off with water regularly, and for indoor plants raise the humidity. Use insecticidal soap if there are a lot. A healthy, unstressed plant shrugs them off.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Discourage mites by spraying plants with a strong stream of water during dry spells and avoiding drought stress; indoors, give good light and some humidity and inspect plants before bringing them in for winter.
pests.prevention_beginner: Hose the plant down now and then in dry weather, and do not let it get badly drought-stressed. Before bringing rosemary indoors for winter, check it over for pests first.

pests.name: Aphids and whiteflies
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Occasional clusters of small soft aphids or tiny white flies on new growth and flowers, most often on stressed or crowded plants and on rosemary brought indoors.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Now and then, small soft insects or tiny white flies on the new growth or flowers, usually on stressed, crowded, or indoor plants.
pests.cause_seasoned: Sap-feeding insects that occasionally find rosemary. Outdoors, healthy plants in full sun rarely have trouble; indoor winter plants are more susceptible.
pests.cause_beginner: Small sap-sucking bugs that sometimes show up, mostly on indoor or stressed plants. Rosemary outdoors in the sun rarely has a problem.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rinse them off with water or use insecticidal soap if numbers rise. Improving airflow and removing nearby stressors usually resolves it.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray them off with water, or use insecticidal soap if there are many. More air and less stress usually fixes it.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Give plants full sun, lean soil, good spacing, and airflow, and avoid overwatering. Vigorous, unstressed rosemary rarely attracts these pests.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep rosemary in full sun with room around it and do not overwater. Healthy plants rarely get these bugs.

pests.name: Spittlebugs
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Frothy white spit-like foam on stems in spring, with a small nymph hidden inside. It looks alarming but rarely harms an established rosemary plant.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Blobs of white froth that look like spit on the stems in spring, with a tiny bug hidden inside. It looks worse than it is.
pests.cause_seasoned: Spittlebug nymphs that shelter inside their own foam while feeding on sap. Numbers are usually low and the damage is mostly cosmetic.
pests.cause_beginner: Young spittlebugs hiding in the foam while they feed. There are usually only a few, and they do little real harm.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock them off with a strong spray of water if you find them unsightly. No treatment is needed for plant health in most cases.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: If the froth bothers you, spray it off with a hose. You usually do not need to do anything else.
pests.prevention_seasoned: No specific prevention is warranted. Good spacing, full sun, and no overwatering keep rosemary vigorous enough to shrug off minor pests.
pests.prevention_beginner: Nothing special is needed. Giving plants room, sun, and not too much water keeps rosemary healthy enough to handle small pests.

diseases.name: Root and crown rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellowing, wilting, browning tips, and dieback that does not recover with watering, often with a darkened, decayed crown at the soil line. It is the disease of concern for rosemary and is tied to wet soil and poor drainage.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Leaves yellow, tips brown, and the plant wilts and dies back even though the soil is wet, often with a dark, rotted spot where the stems meet the ground. This is the main thing that kills rosemary, and it comes from staying too wet.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Water mold pathogens (Phytophthora and related water molds) that thrive in saturated, poorly drained soil and attack the roots and crown. Overwatering and wet feet, not cold, are the underlying cause.
diseases.cause_beginner: A rot that takes hold when soil stays soggy and drains badly, attacking the roots and base. The real cause is too much water, not cold.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once the crown is rotting; remove and discard affected plants. Focus entirely on prevention through drainage rather than rescue.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Once the base is rotting there is no fix, so pull out and throw away affected plants. The answer is preventing it with good drainage, not curing it.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant in sharply drained soil in full sun, water deeply but infrequently, and never let rosemary sit in wet ground. On clay, use a mound or raised bed, and space plants for airflow.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant in well-draining soil in full sun, water deeply but rarely, and never let rosemary sit in soggy ground. On heavy clay, plant on a mound or raised bed and give plants room.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: A white powdery coating on foliage, favored by damp, still, humid air and crowded plants. It is most common on rosemary overwintered indoors and in humid regions, and is minor compared with root and crown rot.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: A white powdery film on the leaves, more likely in damp, still air or on crowded and indoor plants. It is a minor problem next to root rot.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Foliar fungi favored by poor air circulation and humidity. Crowding, low airflow, and stagnant indoor winter conditions raise the risk.
diseases.cause_beginner: A leaf fungus that likes damp, stuffy air with no breeze. Crowding and stale indoor air over winter make it worse.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Improve airflow, thin crowded growth, and space plants; indoors, give good air movement and light. Remove badly affected foliage.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Give the plant more air and space, and for indoor plants keep some air moving. Pick off badly coated leaves.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Good air circulation is the main defense: space plants, site in full sun, avoid overhead watering, and do not crowd indoor winter plants.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Keep air moving around the plant: give it room and full sun, water at the base, and do not crowd it indoors over winter.

pests.name: Spittlebugs
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Frothy white spit-like foam on stems in late spring, with a small nymph hidden inside. It looks alarming but rarely harms an established sage plant.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Blobs of white froth like spit on the stems in late spring, with a tiny bug hidden inside. It looks worse than it is.
pests.cause_seasoned: Spittlebug nymphs sheltering in their own foam while sipping sap. Numbers are usually low and damage is mostly cosmetic.
pests.cause_beginner: Young spittlebugs hiding in the foam while they feed. There are usually only a few, and they do little real harm.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock them off with a strong spray of water if you find them unsightly; no treatment is needed for plant health in most cases.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: If the froth bothers you, spray it off with a hose. You usually do not need to do anything else.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Give plants full sun and airflow and do not overwater; vigorous sage shrugs off minor pests.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep sage in full sun with room around it and do not overwater; healthy plants handle small pests.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine stippling or bronzing of the leaves and faint webbing, most common on plants in hot, dry, dusty conditions or stressed indoor plants.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Leaves look dusty, speckled, or faded, sometimes with fine webbing, usually in hot dry spells or on indoor plants.
pests.cause_seasoned: Tiny sap-sucking mites that build up in hot, dry, still air, especially on dusty or drought-stressed foliage.
pests.cause_beginner: Very small mites that multiply in hot, dry conditions and feed on the leaves.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rinse the foliage with a strong spray of water to knock mites down, repeating every few days; insecticidal soap helps in bad cases.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray the leaves with water every few days to wash the mites off; insecticidal soap works if there are a lot.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Maintain good airflow, hose off dust in hot spells, and avoid drought stress on containers, which invites mites.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep air moving, rinse dust off in hot weather, and do not let potted sage dry out to the point of stress.

pests.name: Slugs and snails
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Ragged holes chewed in leaves and slime trails, mainly on young or newly set plants in damp, shady spots.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Chewed, ragged holes in the leaves and shiny slime trails, mostly on young plants in damp shade.
pests.cause_seasoned: Slugs and snails feeding at night, favored by wet mulch, crowding, and shade around young plants.
pests.cause_beginner: Slugs and snails eating the leaves at night; they like damp, shady, crowded spots.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick at night, remove damp hiding places, and use traps or iron-phosphate bait around vulnerable seedlings.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick them off after dark, clear away damp hiding spots, and use slug traps or an iron-phosphate bait, which carries less risk around pets than the older metaldehyde baits, near young plants.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant in full sun with good drainage and space plants for airflow; a dry, sunny site is unfriendly to slugs.
pests.prevention_beginner: Give sage a sunny, well-drained, open spot; slugs avoid dry, sunny ground.

pests.name: Leafhoppers
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Occasional small hopping insects on the foliage, more likely on stressed or crowded plants than on healthy sage.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Now and then, tiny hopping bugs on the leaves, usually only on stressed or crowded plants.
pests.cause_seasoned: Sap-feeding insects that occasionally find sage; the plant has few serious pests and rarely needs spraying.
pests.cause_beginner: Small sap-sucking insects that sometimes turn up. Sage has few pest problems and rarely needs treatment.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rinse them off with water or use insecticidal soap if numbers climb; improving airflow and removing stress usually resolves it.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray them off with water, or use insecticidal soap for heavy numbers; more air and less stress usually fixes it.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Full sun, lean soil, and good spacing keep sage unstressed and unattractive to these pests.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep sage in full sun with room around it; healthy plants rarely get these bugs.

diseases.name: Root and stem rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Wilting, yellowing, and dieback that does not recover with watering, often with a darkened, decayed base at the soil line. It is the main disease of sage and is tied to wet soil and poor drainage.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Leaves wilt and yellow and the plant dies back even though the soil is wet, often with a dark, rotted spot where the stems meet the ground. This is the main thing that kills sage, and it comes from staying too wet.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soil-borne water molds and fungi that attack the roots and crown of plants sitting in saturated, poorly drained soil. Wet feet and humid heat, not cold, are the underlying cause.
diseases.cause_beginner: A rot that takes hold when soil stays soggy or the weather is hot and muggy, attacking the roots and base. The real cause is wet soil, not cold.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once the crown is rotting; remove and discard affected plants and fix drainage. Focus on prevention, not rescue.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Once the base is rotting there is no fix, so pull out and throw away the plant. The answer is preventing it with good drainage, not curing it.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, water deeply but infrequently, and never let sage sit wet. On clay, use a mound or raised bed and space plants for airflow.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Use well-draining soil in full sun, water deeply but rarely, and never let sage sit in soggy ground. On heavy soil, plant on a mound and give plants room.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: A white to gray powdery film on the leaves, most likely in humid weather or on crowded, poorly ventilated plants. It weakens the plant and taints the flavor but is rarely fatal.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: A dusty white coating on the leaves, more likely in muggy weather or on crowded plants. It does not usually kill sage but makes it look and taste worse.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Fungi favored by warm, humid, still air, especially where plants are crowded or shaded. Damp, stagnant conditions raise the risk.
diseases.cause_beginner: Fungi that like warm, damp, still air around crowded plants. Poor airflow makes it worse.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves, thin for airflow, and avoid overhead watering; the spring prune also opens up the canopy.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick off the coated leaves, give the plant more air, and water at the soil instead of over the top. The spring trim helps too.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants well, site in full sun, avoid overhead watering, and prune to keep the plant open. Airflow is the main defense.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Leave room between plants, plant in full sun, water at the base, and trim to keep it open. Good air movement is the key.

diseases.name: Verticillium wilt
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Sudden wilting and yellowing of branches, sometimes on one side of the plant, that does not recover; a soil-borne wilt that can persist in the ground.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Branches wilt and yellow, often on one side, and do not bounce back. It is a soil disease that can stay in the ground.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A soil-borne fungus that plugs the plant's water-conducting tissue. It builds up in soils where susceptible plants are grown repeatedly.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus in the soil that blocks the plant's water pipes. It builds up where the same kinds of plants grow year after year.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure; remove affected plants and avoid replanting sage or other susceptible crops in the same spot. Improve drainage and airflow.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no fix once a plant has it, so remove it and do not replant sage in the same spot. Better drainage and airflow help.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant in well-drained soil, rotate the planting site when starting new plants, and avoid ground with a history of wilt.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Use well-drained soil, and start new sage in a fresh spot rather than where a wilted plant grew.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine stippling or yellowing on the tiny leaves and faint webbing on the stems, most likely in hot, dry weather or on stressed or crowded plants. Thyme is generally pest-resistant, so this is usually a minor, weather-driven problem.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny yellow speckles on the leaves and faint webbing on the stems, usually in hot, dry weather. Thyme rarely has pest trouble, so this is normally minor.
pests.cause_seasoned: Tiny sap-feeding mites that flare in hot, dry conditions. Thyme has few pests overall and is typically grown with little or no pesticide.
pests.cause_beginner: Very small sap-sucking mites that show up in hot, dry spells. Thyme has very few pest problems and rarely needs spraying.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rinse plants with a strong spray of water, and use insecticidal soap if numbers climb. A hard harvest or shear removes much of the infested growth at once.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray them off with water, and use insecticidal soap if there are a lot. Cutting the plant back also removes most of them.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Give plants full sun and good spacing for airflow and avoid drought-stressing container plants in heat. Vigorous, unstressed thyme rarely attracts mites.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep thyme in full sun with room around it, and do not let potted plants bake bone-dry in a heat wave. Healthy plants rarely get mites.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Occasional clusters of small soft-bodied insects on tender new growth, most likely on stressed or overcrowded plants. Rarely a serious problem on thyme.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Now and then, small soft bugs on new growth, usually only on plants that are stressed or crowded. Rarely a big deal on thyme.
pests.cause_seasoned: Sap-feeding insects that occasionally find thyme. As with mites, thyme is fairly pest-resistant and seldom needs treatment.
pests.cause_beginner: Small sap-sucking insects that sometimes appear. Thyme has very few pest problems and rarely needs spraying.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rinse them off with water or use insecticidal soap if numbers build. Improving airflow and removing stress usually resolves it.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray them off with water, or use insecticidal soap if there are a lot. More air and less stress usually fixes it.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Full sun, lean soil, good spacing, and no overwatering keep thyme vigorous enough to shrug off aphids.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep thyme in full sun with room around it, dry lean soil, and not too much water. Healthy plants rarely get aphids.

diseases.name: Root and crown rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellowing, wilting, and dieback that does not recover with watering, often with a darkened, decayed base at the soil line. It is the main way thyme is lost and is tied to wet, poorly drained soil rather than to cold.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Leaves yellow and the plant wilts and dies back even though the soil is wet, often with a dark, rotted spot at the base. This is the main thing that kills thyme, and it comes from staying too wet.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soilborne rots that thrive in saturated, poorly drained soil and attack the roots and crown. Waterlogged ground, not cold, is the underlying cause; thyme is intolerant of wet feet.
diseases.cause_beginner: A rot that takes hold when soil stays soggy and drains badly, attacking the roots and base. The real cause is wet soil, not cold weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once the crown is rotting; remove and discard affected plants. Focus everything on prevention through drainage rather than rescue.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Once the base is rotting there is no fix, so pull out and throw away affected plants. The answer is preventing it with good drainage, not curing it.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant in sharply drained, lean soil in full sun, keep plants on the dry side, and never let thyme sit in wet ground. On clay or in humid regions, use a mound or raised bed and space plants for airflow.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant in fast-draining soil in full sun, keep it on the dry side, and never let thyme sit in soggy ground. On heavy clay or in humid areas, plant on a mound or raised bed and give plants room.

diseases.name: Foliar fungal problems in humid weather
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Powdery-white coating, spotting, or grayish moldy patches on the foliage, favored by warm, humid, still air and on crowded or overhead-watered plants. A minor issue next to root and crown rot.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: A powdery white film, spots, or grayish mold on the leaves in warm, humid weather, more likely on crowded plants. A minor problem next to root rot.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Foliar fungi such as powdery mildew that are favored by humidity, crowding, and poor air movement. Thyme is fairly disease-resistant, so these are mainly a humid-climate and overcrowding issue.
diseases.cause_beginner: Leaf fungi like powdery mildew that like damp, still, humid air and crowded plants. Thyme is fairly disease-resistant, so this is mostly a humid-weather problem.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected foliage, open up airflow, and water at the base rather than overhead. A hard harvest or post-bloom shear clears and renews the canopy.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick off affected leaves, give the plant more air, and water at the soil instead of over the top. Cutting it back also helps.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants for air circulation, site in full sun, avoid overhead watering, and favor the taller, smooth-leaved culinary types over low woolly ones where humidity is high. Good airflow is the main defense.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Give plants room for airflow, plant in full sun, and avoid watering over the leaves. In humid areas, the upright leafy types handle it better than the low fuzzy ones.
